questions.stem: The modern periodic table is based on which property of elements?
options: Number of electrons in valence shell only
questions.explanation: Modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number (Moseley's law, 1913). Earlier (Mendeleev, 1869) used atomic mass, but this gave inversions (e.g., Te before I despite higher mass). Atomic number determines chemical properties because it equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom, which determines electron configuration. The atomic number is also a stable property; atomic mass varies with isotopes.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The modern periodic table has how many periods (horizontal rows)?
questions.explanation: The modern periodic table has 7 periods (horizontal rows) and 18 groups (vertical columns). Period 1 has only 2 elements (H, He); Period 2 and 3 have 8 each; Periods 4 and 5 have 18 each; Periods 6 and 7 have 32 each (including 14 lanthanides and 14 actinides shown separately). The period number = principal quantum number n of the outermost shell being filled.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Elements in Group 1 (alkali metals) include:
options: Lithium, Sodium, Potassium, Rubidium, Caesium, Francium
questions.explanation: Group 1 alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr (and H is also in Group 1 but is a non-metal — sometimes considered separately). All have one valence electron (ns¹), are highly reactive (especially with water), soft enough to cut with a knife, low density, low melting points. Reactivity increases down the group. Group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca...) are alkaline earth metals. Group 17 (F, Cl, Br...) are halogens.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Group 18 elements (noble gases) include:
options: Helium, Neon, Argon, Krypton, Xenon, Radon
questions.explanation: Group 18 (noble gases / inert gases): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og (Oganesson). All have full outer shells (1s² for He; ns²np⁶ for others) — extremely stable, generally unreactive. Uses: He (balloons, MRI cooling), Ne (signs), Ar (welding shields, light bulb fill), Kr (lasers, flash lamps), Xe (headlamp lights, anaesthesia), Rn (radioactive, hazardous in basements). Xenon and Krypton can form some compounds; helium and neon are truly inert.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Group 17 elements are called halogens. The most reactive halogen is:
questions.explanation: Fluorine (F) is the most reactive halogen — and one of the most reactive elements overall. Reactivity DECREASES down Group 17: F > Cl > Br > I > At. This is because F has the smallest atomic radius, so the nucleus attracts incoming electrons most strongly. F is so reactive it reacts even with glass and most metals at room temperature. Cl is reactive enough to disinfect water. Br is liquid at room temp; I is solid.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Lanthanides and actinides are also known as:
questions.explanation: Lanthanides (atomic numbers 57-71, Ce to Lu) and Actinides (89-103, Th to Lr) are f-block elements because their differentiating electrons fill the f-orbitals. They're called 'inner transition elements'. Lanthanides are mostly stable; actinides are largely radioactive (Th, U, Pu are best known). All lanthanides have similar chemistry due to 'lanthanide contraction' (steady decrease in atomic radius across the series).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Mendeleev published his original periodic table in:
questions.explanation: Dmitri Mendeleev (Russian) published his first periodic table in 1869, arranging 63 known elements by atomic mass and chemical properties. He famously LEFT GAPS for elements he predicted but were not yet discovered (Ga, Ge, Sc) — and accurately predicted their properties; these elements were discovered within his lifetime, confirming his table. Henry Moseley (1913) reordered the table by atomic number, fixing inversions caused by isotopic mass averages.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Across a period (left to right), atomic radius generally:
options: Decreases due to increasing effective nuclear charge attracting electrons closer
questions.explanation: Across a period, electrons are added to the same shell while protons are added to the nucleus. The added electrons don't significantly shield each other, so effective nuclear charge increases, pulling electrons inward. Atomic radius DECREASES from left to right. Example in Period 2: Li (152 pm) > Be (112 pm) > B (85 pm) > C (77 pm) > N (75 pm) > O (73 pm) > F (71 pm). Going DOWN a group, atomic radius INCREASES because new electron shells are added.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Ionisation energy (first IE) generally:
options: Decreases across a period and increases down a group
Increases across a period and decreases down a group
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy = energy needed to remove the outermost electron. Across a period, atomic radius decreases and nuclear charge increases, so the outermost electron is held more tightly → IE INCREASES. Down a group, electrons are in higher shells (farther from nucleus, more shielded) → IE DECREASES. Highest IE: Helium (~2372 kJ/mol). Lowest IE: Caesium and Francium (alkali metals at bottom-left). Trends help predict chemical reactivity.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Electronegativity (Pauling scale) is highest for which element?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (Pauling scale: 3.98). Electronegativity = tendency to attract bonding electrons. Top-right of the periodic table = highest EN; bottom-left = lowest. Trend across a period: increases (more nuclear pull). Trend down a group: decreases (more shielding). Caesium has the lowest EN (~0.79). Difference in EN determines bond polarity: small difference = covalent, large difference (~>1.7) = ionic.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The element with atomic number 26 is:
questions.explanation: Iron (Fe) has atomic number 26. It's a Period 4, Group 8 transition metal. Configuration: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Iron is the most abundant metal in Earth's core and crust (after aluminium for the crust). It's biologically essential — central atom of hemoglobin (oxygen transport). Symbol 'Fe' from Latin 'ferrum'. **Short Trick:** Common transition metals to memorise: Cr(24), Mn(25), Fe(26), Co(27), Ni(28), Cu(29), Zn(30).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Mendeleev's periodic table predicted properties of which then-undiscovered elements (which he called 'eka-' elements)?
questions.explanation: Mendeleev left gaps for predicted elements and named them with 'eka-' (Sanskrit for 'one') prefix denoting position relative to known elements. Eka-aluminium (predicted 1869, discovered 1875 as Gallium by Lecoq); eka-silicon (predicted 1869, discovered 1886 as Germanium by Winkler); eka-boron (predicted 1869, discovered 1879 as Scandium by Nilson). Predicted properties (mass, density, melting point, chemical behaviour) matched observations remarkably well — the dramatic confirmation of his table.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Transition metals (d-block) commonly exhibit which characteristic NOT typical of main group metals?
options: They show variable oxidation states (e.g., Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺; Cu⁺, Cu²⁺) due to easy involvement of d-electrons
They have very low melting points
questions.explanation: Transition metals (d-block, Groups 3-12) have partially filled d-orbitals, which give them characteristic properties: (1) Variable oxidation states — Fe (+2, +3), Mn (+2 to +7), Cu (+1, +2); (2) Colored compounds (d-d electron transitions absorb visible light); (3) Catalytic activity (Fe in Haber process, Pt in catalytic converters); (4) Form complex ions (with ligands); (5) Paramagnetic in many states; (6) High melting points and densities.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an alkaline earth metal?
questions.explanation: Alkaline earth metals are Group 2: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra. They have two valence electrons (ns²), are silvery, denser than alkali metals, and less reactive but still reactive enough to be stored carefully. Aluminium is in Group 13 (p-block), not Group 2 — it's a post-transition metal. **Short Trick:** Alkaline earth metals all end in -ium except Beryllium and Magnesium are easy to remember as Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The diagonal relationship in the periodic table refers to similarity between:
options: Elements in the same group only
Elements diagonally adjacent in periods 2 and 3 (e.g., Li-Mg, Be-Al, B-Si)
questions.explanation: Diagonal relationship: certain pairs of elements one period and one group apart show similar chemical properties due to similar charge densities (charge/radius ratio). Key pairs: Li ↔ Mg (both react with N₂ to form nitrides; carbonates decompose on heating), Be ↔ Al (both amphoteric oxides, dissolve in alkali), B ↔ Si (both form acidic oxides, similar covalent character). This is a notable exception to the general 'down-the-group' similarity pattern.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The 'p-block' of the periodic table comprises which groups?
questions.explanation: Blocks of the periodic table by orbital being filled: s-block (Groups 1-2 + He): outermost ns orbital. p-block (Groups 13-18): outermost np orbital. d-block (Groups 3-12, transition metals): (n-1)d orbital. f-block (Lanthanides and Actinides): (n-2)f orbital. p-block contains a mix of metals (Al, Sn, Pb), metalloids (B, Si, Ge), and non-metals (C, N, O, F, ...). The 'staircase' separating metals from non-metals runs through the p-block.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Which is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Most abundant elements in Earth's crust by mass: Oxygen (~46%) > Silicon (~28%) > Aluminium (~8%) > Iron (~5%) > Calcium (~4%) > Sodium (~2.8%) > Potassium (~2.6%) > Magnesium (~2%). Oxygen dominates because it's in nearly all rocks as silicates and oxides (SiO₂ = quartz/sand). The CORE is mostly iron, but the crust is dominated by lighter elements. In the entire universe, hydrogen dominates (~74%).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Metalloids (elements with both metallic and non-metallic properties) include:
options: Boron, Silicon, Germanium, Arsenic, Antimony, Tellurium
questions.explanation: Metalloids occupy the 'staircase' diagonal in the p-block: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, At (sometimes Po). They have intermediate properties — semiconductors of electricity (basis for the entire semiconductor industry: Si chips, Ge transistors), lustrous like metals but brittle like non-metals. Silicon is the most economically important: solar cells, computer chips, glass. Boron is essential for plants. Antimony is used in flame retardants.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Henry Moseley's contribution (1913) to the periodic table was:
options: Showing that atomic NUMBER (not atomic mass) is the fundamental property that orders elements, by measuring X-ray frequencies emitted by elements
Proposing the first electron shell model
questions.explanation: Henry Moseley (1887–1915, killed at Gallipoli in WWI) bombarded elements with high-energy electrons and measured the X-ray frequencies they emitted. He found that √(frequency) varied linearly with a whole number — the atomic number Z (= number of protons). This proved that atomic NUMBER, not atomic mass, is the fundamental ordering property of elements, fixing the few mass-based inversions in Mendeleev's table (e.g., Te < I by mass but Te has lower Z).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that the third electron shell (n=3) can hold?
questions.explanation: Maximum electrons in shell n = 2n². For n=3: 2(3)² = 18 electrons. The shells fill: n=1: 2 electrons (1s²); n=2: 8 electrons (2s² 2p⁶); n=3: 18 electrons (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰); n=4: 32 electrons (4s² 4p⁶ 4d¹⁰ 4f¹⁴). However, the 3d subshell fills only AFTER 4s (Aufbau principle), so Period 3 elements use just 3s and 3p (8 electrons). The 3d sub-shell holds electrons starting from Period 4.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Among elements Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al — which has the LARGEST atomic radius?
questions.explanation: K is in Period 4 (n=4), the others are in Period 3 (n=3). Period 4 elements have an extra shell, so they're larger. Among Period 4 alkali metals, K is on the far left (largest in its period). Atomic radii (pm): Na 186, K 227, Mg 160, Ca 197, Al 143. **Short Trick:** Atomic radius increases DOWN a group and DECREASES across a period. Bottom-left of periodic table = largest atoms (Cs, Fr).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Why is the first ionisation energy of Nitrogen (N, IE₁ = 1402 kJ/mol) HIGHER than that of Oxygen (O, IE₁ = 1314 kJ/mol), despite Oxygen being further to the right?
options: Nitrogen has more protons than Oxygen

Nitrogen has a half-filled 2p³ subshell (extra stability); removing an electron from O disrupts a paired electron pair in 2p⁴, which is energetically easier than breaking the stable half-filled configuration of N
Oxygen has fewer total electrons than Nitrogen
The trend is actually monotonic — this is a measurement error
questions.explanation: Nitrogen's electron config is 1s²2s²2p³ — the three 2p electrons each occupy a separate orbital (Hund's rule), giving a stable half-filled configuration. Removing an electron breaks this stability — costly. Oxygen is 1s²2s²2p⁴ — the 4th p-electron must pair up in an orbital, experiencing electron-electron repulsion. Removing this paired electron is easier (relieves repulsion). So IE(N) > IE(O), a notable exception to the general increasing-across-period trend. Same pattern: IE(P) > IE(S).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The 'aufbau principle' for filling electron orbitals follows the order:
options: By increasing energy, following the (n+l) rule: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p
Random order — orbitals fill in whichever order is convenient
questions.explanation: Aufbau principle (German for 'building up'): electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy, determined by the (n+l) rule. When two orbitals have the same (n+l), the one with smaller n fills first. So 4s (n+l = 4+0 = 4) fills BEFORE 3d (n+l = 3+2 = 5), even though 3d has lower n. The diagonal mnemonic: 1s → 2s → 2p,3s → 3p,4s → 3d,4p,5s → 4d,5p,6s → 4f,5d,6p,7s → 5f,6d,7p. This explains why Period 4 starts with K (4s) before transition metals (3d).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Why does Copper (Cu) have the anomalous electron configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ instead of the expected [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²?
options: The 3d orbital is at higher energy than 4s for copper
A fully-filled 3d¹⁰ subshell offers extra stability that outweighs the cost of having only one 4s electron, so copper 'borrows' a 4s electron to complete 3d
Copper has more protons than expected
This is a measurement error and copper actually has 3d⁹ 4s²
questions.explanation: Copper (Z=29) has configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ — anomalous because filled subshells (3d¹⁰) and half-filled subshells (e.g., 3d⁵) have extra exchange-energy stability. By promoting one 4s electron to 3d, Cu achieves both fully-filled 3d¹⁰ AND a half-filled 4s¹, giving a lower-energy ground state than the 'expected' 3d⁹ 4s². Same anomaly for Chromium: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²). These exceptions help explain Cu's distinctive chemistry and Cr's reactivity.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: The most recently officially named elements (2016 IUPAC additions) completing Period 7 are:
questions.explanation: In November 2016, IUPAC officially named four new elements completing the 7th period: Nihonium (Nh, Z=113, after Japan/Nihon, discovered at RIKEN), Moscovium (Mc, Z=115, after Moscow region/JINR Dubna), Tennessine (Ts, Z=117, after Tennessee/Oak Ridge), Oganesson (Og, Z=118, after Yuri Oganessian — the first time an element was named after a living person). All are super-heavy, synthetic, highly radioactive with half-lives of milliseconds. They complete the p-block of Period 7.
questions.subject: Chemistry
